blocks.text: [II, 693] In the crowing of the cock there are two marvels. One is that so small an animal crows with so strained a voice that it is heard from very far away. The other is that it crows at fixed hours, and at the very time when the other birds give themselves to sleep. The former is wonderfully extolled by the Talmudists in the tractate Yoma, fol. 20b, where someone says of the sacred cock at Jerusalem: והיה קולו נשמע משלוש פרסאות מעשה באגריפס המלך שהיה בא בדרך ושמע קולו בשלוש פרסאות וכשבא לביתו שיגר לו מתנות, Its voice was heard from three parasangs. Let King Agrippa serve as an example: while he was on a journey, he heard it from three parasangs, and when he had come home, he sent it gifts. This is slight compared with what another says in the same place: ונשמע קולו ביריחו, its voice was heard as far as Jericho. For, as Rabbi Yochanan asserts, מירושלם ליריחו עשרה פרסי, From the city of Jerusalem to Jericho there are ten parasangs. These things are indeed fabulous; but truer is what Cardano says, De subtilitate book 10: The cock, if it were a rare animal, would be worthy of admiration not only for its form but for its crowing. It exults with its voice, and it is heard far off: at night even a thousand paces and more. Of its nocturnal crowing at fixed hours Alkazuinius says: ومن عجايب معرفته ساعات الليل فان الليل اذا كان خمسة عشر ساعه يقسط اصواته عليها كما كان يقسطه عليها وهو تسع ساعات وذلك بالهام من الله [wa-min ʿajāyib maʿrifatuhu sāʿāt al-layl fa-inna al-layl idhā kāna khamsata ʿashar sāʿa yuqassiṭ aṣwātahu ʿalayhā kamā kāna yuqassiṭuhu ʿalayhā wa-huwa tisʿ sāʿāt wa-dhālika bi-ilhām min Allāh] [II, 694] Among the marvels (of its nature is this), that it knows the hours of the night: so that, when the night is of fifteen hours, it apportions its crowings in proportion to it; just as it also apportions them when it is of only nine hours, and this by the inspiration of God. And Damir: واعظم ما فيه من العجايب معرفه الاوقات [col. 124] الليلية فيقسط اصواته عليها تقسيطا لا يكاد يغادر منه شيا سوا طال او قصر ويوالي صياحه قبل الفجر وبعده فسبحان من هداه لذلك [wa-aʿẓam mā fīhi min al-ʿajāyib maʿrifat al-awqāt al-layliyya fa-yuqassiṭ aṣwātahu ʿalayhā taqsīṭan lā yakādu yughādir minhu shayʾan sawāʾ ṭāla aw qaṣura wa-yuwālī ṣiyāḥahu qabl al-fajr wa-baʿdahu fa-subḥān man hadāhu li-dhālika] The most marvellous thing in it is that it knows the times of the night, and according to them distributes its crowings with so even a balance that it omits hardly anything of them, whether they be longer or shorter. And its crowing continually precedes and follows the dawn. Praise be to Him who taught it this. From the Chronicles of Isfahan we shall show in its place that Muhammad, seeking the causes of so great a thing, took refuge in fables. For he imagines that God has a white cock whose wings are adorned with emeralds, jacinths and pearls and spread from east to west, whose head is beneath the throne of glory and whose feet are in the highest air; and that it thus announces the time of prayer every morning and is heard by all the inhabitants of heaven and earth except men and demons. And therefore, he says, يجيبه ديوك الارض [yujībuhu duyūk al-arḍ] the cocks of the earth answer it. We have shown that this was partly taken from the Hebrews. But among the Greeks too Callisthenes recognizes something divine in the crowing of the cock. Hence Cicero, De Divinatione book 2: What came into Callisthenes' mind, to say that the gods gave cocks the signal to crow? Yet in the same author Democritus explains in excellent words the cause why cocks crow before daylight. For when the food has been driven out of the breast, distributed through the whole body and assimilated, they utter their crowings, satisfied with rest. And in our own age a very learned man writes: It crows chiefly about the midnight, or just before sunrise. That is, partly when the sun has completed half of its nocturnal course, partly from the time when it has reached, or nearly reached, our horizon, the cock's senses are released. For this animal, by a force of nature, or from a property of its temperament, is so affected by the sun that it then wakes up. Rejoicing, therefore, both in the rest it has sweetly enjoyed and because it feels that its breast or stomach is not weighed down by food as before (since this has now been digested through the whole body), it attests its joy by crowing and by clapping its wings. At the same time also, because the cock's warm and thin blood, through the nocturnal condition of the air, has raised exhalations and vapours in the muscles, it therefore claps its wings and, singing with its throat, strives to dispel the vapours together with the phlegm gathered by the cold of the night, just as other animals expel wind by stretching or yawning. Of this I approve only the statement that this animal is affected by the sun. But why it is affected by the sun is the very thing in question, and indeed sought in vain, since it depends on a hidden property of nature. For as to what is alleged about joy felt from the digestion of food: if it were true, then, since in a healthy cock digestion is as quick [II, 695] or even quicker in winter than in summer, because the heat of the stomach by which food is digested is then more intense, the winter cockcrow would not be later than the summer one. But the matter is quite otherwise. For the morning crowing of the cock here takes place in winter three or four hours later than in summer. And the same reasoning applies to the other things they add here. So the question must be investigated further.
